narration:
The organiser is a broad, grey-haired woman with ink on her thumb and a ledger tucked under one arm. She hears you out to the last word without blinking, then pins a fresh notice to the board.

"Free," she says. "Now." She taps the tack in with her thumb. "Lad, the last *hero* who passed through here took three silver off the miller up front, to clear the wolves out of his weir. That was in spring. The miller's still waiting, and so are the wolves."

She turns to face you properly. She isn't hostile, just very hard to impress.

"Nobody gets paid up front on my board. Not heroes, not my own nephew. You get paid when the work's done and someone I trust says it's done." She runs a finger down the ledger. "But if you want the best-paid job, here it is. The spring flood shifted the marker stakes on the Fennick causeway, and the salt carter won't take his wagon across without someone who can find the true road. Thirty silver on delivery at Brindle Ford. Two days there, if the ground holds."

Her eyes drop for a moment to the compass at your belt, then come back up.

"That's the offer. My name's Marta Hollin. I don't do discounts, and I don't do favours for strangers. Not yet, anyway."

narration:
The notice board falls behind you, its papers curling in the wet. Rain comes down steady and cold, and the only warm light on the street spills from a low stone building with a lantern swinging over the door. The painted sign shows a ladle crossed with a key: **the Ladle & Key**.

Inside it smells of peat smoke, wet wool and something with onions in it. A handful of drinkers sit near the hearth. Two of them are drovers, still muddy to the knee. They glance at you and go back to their cups. You shake out your cloak by the door, and the rain spatters across the flagstones.

Behind the bar a broad woman with her sleeves rolled to the elbow is wiping out a pot. She takes in your boots, your cloak and your empty hands, all in one look.

"Hot?" She nods toward a black kettle-pot on a hook by the fire. "Barley and mutton, last of it. Two coppers a bowl, bread included. Ale's one. Kitchen shuts when that pot's scraped, so don't think about it too long."

She sets down the pot. "And if you mean hot as in *news*, the river's up over the causeway, and the ferryman won't cross in the dark. So half the road's sleeping in my common room tonight, and old Bramwell the carter is in the corner cursing it." She jerks her chin toward a grey-bearded man hunched over a cold pipe. "Says he'll pay anyone who knows the high track round the marsh. Nobody here does."

She looks back at you, eyebrows raised. "So. Stew?"

narration:
The innkeeper is nearest, and she doesn't stop wiping the pot while you ask. "Honest work." She looks you over again, longer this time. "This week the honest work is mostly mud. Once the water drops there'll be fence-mending and ditch-clearing from here to the mill. Brask the ferryman will want hands to drag his landing stage back out of the reeds, and he pays in silver if he's in a good mood. He hasn't been in a good mood since spring."

One of the drovers by the hearth snorts into his cup. "Grazier up at Holloway lost a dozen ewes to the flood. He'll pay for anyone who finds them alive. Or dead, so he can stop wondering."

"That's next week's work, though." The innkeeper sets the pot down and folds her arms. "Tonight's work is in that corner."

The old carter has heard every word. He takes the cold pipe out of his teeth and points the stem at the window, where rain is hissing down the glass.

"First light," Bramwell says to the whole room, loud and sour. "I'm going at first light, guide or no guide. Damn this rain. Damn that river. Damn the high track and whoever forgot to put a road on it." He clamps the pipe back in his teeth. "Cheese won't wait for the weather to apologise."

The innkeeper's eyes come back to you, and to your empty hands. "And if you've no coin for stew, I've a woodpile out back that wants splitting and a pot that wants scrubbing. Same price."

The ford road narrows between a drainage ditch and a low bank. Behind you, the square’s lamplight fades; ahead, reeds crowd the road where it slopes toward running water.

You keep your pace measured, watching the gaps between the stems. The water’s steady noise could cover a quiet footstep.

“Mind the left edge.”

The voice comes from scarcely six paces away. Only when a man rises from behind a clump of reeds do you distinguish him from the bank. He has seen you first.

He lifts a shuttered lantern. Its light catches a long wooden pole, muddy boots, and a bite of collapsed earth beside the road.

“Lost that bit of bank yesterday. Looks solid in the dark.”

narration:
Marta Hollin stops writing. She lifts her pen off the page, and for a moment the whole square seems to wait with her.

"Her," she says. "Not *his*. And no."

She shuts the ledger over one finger to keep her place. "There's no key, lad. It's a board. It has tacks in it. Anyone who can read can read it, and anyone who can't asks me." She glances down at her belt, where a plain leather purse hangs, then back at you. "And that's my money. Asking for it in front of witnesses, in daylight, has a name round here. It isn't 'hero.'"

Behind you, the carters who stayed to watch the wrestling have stopped talking. Ferrin is still brushing dust off his smock. He doesn't step forward, but he stops brushing, and he doesn't look like he's joking anymore.

Marta doesn't call anyone over. She doesn't need to.

"Here's how it goes," she says, in the same unhurried voice. "You walk off now, sleep off whatever this is, and you're at Oswin Tarrow's wagon at first light, sober and civil. Then the causeway job's still yours, and I'll forget I heard this. Or you keep at it, and I send word to Oswin tonight that he'd do better crossing alone."

She opens the ledger again and finds her line.

"Your choice. I've got work to do."

The organiser is a broad woman in a waxed coat with chalk dust worked into the creases of her knuckles. She finishes the line she is writing on her slate before she looks up. She looks at your boots first, then the compass, then your face.

"Hero," she repeats, as if she's weighing the word on a grocer's scale. "Last hero who wanted paying before working had a very fine sword. He took three silver off me for the mill-race job. The mill-race is still blocked. I expect the sword's been sold."

narration:
The rain follows Rowan off the square and down two crooked lanes until a lit window shows through it. A tin sign creaks over a low stone doorway, painted with a candle hanging from a hook: **the Tallow Hook**.

Inside, the air is thick with peat smoke and wet wool. Three late drinkers sit near the hearth, where a grey dog lies so close to the coals it ought to be smoking. Behind the counter a broad woman in her fifties, sleeves pushed past the elbow, is wiping down the last of the mugs. She watches Rowan's cloak drip onto her floorboards.

"What's hot," she repeats, sounding drily amused. "At this hour? The bottom of the pot. Barley and mutton, on since noon, thick enough to stand a spoon in. Three coppers a bowl, bread with it. Cider's warming by the fire for two more." She puts the mug down. "Coin first after midnight. Nothing personal. The last fellow ate twice and left through the privy window."

At the hearth, an old man in a drover's coat goes back to whatever he was complaining about, loud enough to carry. "I'm telling you, the cairns on the moor road are half washed down. Ewan won't find the ford in this. Nobody's getting peat till it dries."

The innkeeper's eyes go to the black window, just for a moment, then back to Rowan. "Well? Bowl or no bowl?"

narration:
The innkeeper is the nearest. She hears the question out without putting down her mug.

"Asking about work before you've answered about the bowl." Her eyes go to Rowan's hands, then to the boots. "That usually tells me how the bowl goes." She sets the mug on the shelf and picks up another. "The board on the square has what it has. Ditching, after this rain. Somebody's wall came down on Fenwick Lane. Pays in coppers and complaints."

"Honest work," the old drover snorts, twisting round in his chair by the hearth. "There's a man sitting out on the moor in the pitch dark with a cartload of peat. That's honest. Go and fetch him."

"Hob." She says only his name, and says it flat.

"Ah, Odile, it's true and you know it."

She wipes the new mug for longer than it needs. "Ewan Dray. He carts my peat down from the cuttings. Should've been in by dark." This time she doesn't look at the window, and that says almost as much. "I'm not asking anyone to go up there tonight. The cairns are down, the ford's high, and I don't need two lost men. At first light I'll send the Corrie lads." She pauses. "But if somebody walked in tomorrow with Ewan and the cart both, that's a silver, plus a bed and supper. Nothing personal. That's just what it's worth to me."

Hob mutters into his cup. "What you need is someone who can find north with no stars out."

By the coals, the grey dog sighs in its sleep.

narration:
Your shoulder still throbs where Osk put you in the packed dirt a few minutes ago, and the carters are still grinning about it over their tailboards. So when you turn on Ilse and order her to hand over her purse and the key to the board, the words don't carry far past the lantern light.

She finishes the line on her slate. Then she looks at you properly, the way she'd look at a cart with a cracked axle.

"It's a board," she says. "It has nails. Nobody's ever needed a key for a nail." She tucks the slate under her arm. Her free hand doesn't go anywhere near her coat. "And my purse is mine. I earned what's in it the slow way."

Behind you, a sack of salt thumps down. Osk doesn't come any closer. He just stops loading, and so do the two carters nearest him.

"Ground's soft tonight, friend," he says, without much of a grin. "Don't go looking for more of it."

"That's twice tonight you've asked for something for nothing," Ilse says, quite level. "There won't be a third time. If there is, Osk walks you to the road and I chalk your face on the slate so the next square hears about you too."

She jerks her chin at the smeared notice on its bent nail. "Dorran still leaves at first light. If you want his twelve silver, go and ask him yourself. I'm not putting my name to you."

Then she goes back to her chalk. You notice the barley stall by the trough is still lit.

He clears a loose pebble from a patch of level ground with his boot. The organiser lifts the notices out of reach.

“No punches. No twisting fingers,” the porter says. “First back to the ground loses.”

He steps forward to meet your challenge—but your victory isn’t certain yet. He has thick forearms and keeps his weight low as you close for a grip.

The porter gives ground half a step, then turns his hip across your path. His grip tightens; your feet leave their footing.

You land flat on your back. He keeps hold of your arm through the fall, checking it enough to spare your head. Dust rises around you.

“Anyone,” he repeats, breathless now, rather than effortless.

The organiser glances over the edge of the notices. “Mind you brush off before inspecting my roads.”

The porter releases your arm and offers a hand up. “Good of you to actually take hold. Most just talk.”

narration:
You lean in close enough to smell lamp oil on his coat and keep your voice under the hiss of the lantern. Whatever he owes, you can help. But only if he tells you the truth, and he has to do it now.

The Pellow-lad story is still hanging between you: a farm boy courting a girl from the ford, he'd said, nothing worth a second look. But at the word *owe*, Corran Hale goes completely still. His hand doesn't go to the ledger this time. It stays flat against his side, and that looks like it's costing him effort.

arguments.name: Marrow Ford
arguments.description: A riverside settlement two days east of Wayside square on foot by the main road. Low houses cluster around the near-bank landing. Whitewashed posts mark the ford; on Rowan's arrival, high water covers the stepping stones and a chain closes the approach. A posted notice directs travellers to the ferry, which resumes service at first light. The ferry is moored beneath a timber shelter on the near bank. A small public house stands farther up the street.

arguments.value: Marrow Ford lies two days east of Wayside square on foot along the main road, through fields and stony uplands to the river. Rowan travelled this route without a toll or transaction. Rain on the second day; westbound timber wagons churned the road. Arrived tired and hungry, with ordinary travel wear but no mechanical injury or exhaustion imposed.
